slides.title: An unfinished plan should not reach the presenter
keyPoints: A title and 1–3 activities are required
Each activity lasts 1–60 minutes
A finished plan totals at most 90 minutes
slides.narration: A session planner collects choices one at a time. A user types a title, adds an activity, and perhaps adds two more. The presenter should receive a ready plan, not a half-filled form. Our rules cover several kinds of information: the title cannot be empty, the number of activities must be between one and three, each duration must be between one and sixty, and the total cannot exceed ninety. A draft can temporarily fail some of those whole-plan rules while the user edits it. The design problem is therefore not simply storing fields. It is making the moment of readiness visible so other code can trust a finished plan.
actions: Classify each rule as a field rule, count rule, or whole-plan rule.
Ask when the presenter should be allowed to see the object.

question.prompt: Why can a valid individual activity still belong to an invalid plan?
question.answer: Two 60-minute activities each satisfy the individual duration rule, but their 120-minute total violates the finished-plan limit.

slides.title: A draft and a product make different promises
keyPoints: A draft may be incomplete
A published plan must satisfy every rule
Readiness belongs at a clear API boundary
slides.narration: An invariant is a rule that must remain true at a stated boundary. The builder's draft does not promise to be ready. It promises only that accepted individual steps have met their local rules. The finished Plan has a stronger promise: it is complete and within the total limit. If both states use one publicly mutable structure, every consumer must remember which state it received and whether validation was already done. The Builder pattern separates these duties. One object gathers choices; another represents a valid result. This is useful when inputs arrive in stages. If all required values arrive together in one small call, a checked constructor may be simpler.
actions: State the weaker draft promise and stronger product promise separately.
Ask why two different types can make a caller’s reasoning easier.

question.prompt: Must the builder reject a draft as soon as its total exceeds 90?
question.answer: Not under this chapter’s policy. Individual steps may create an overlong draft, but build must reject it before a Plan is published.

slides.title: A public draft works when one caller stays careful
keyPoints: A struct groups related values
Validation is an ordinary function
A later edit can invalidate an earlier result
slides.narration: This small design can be perfectly reasonable inside one local workflow. Draft groups a string and a list of integer durations. The valid function reads through a const reference and checks every rule. std::accumulate adds the durations, beginning from zero. The caller checks before printing, so the first output is a fifty-minute Review plan. Then the caller clears the title. The same object is now invalid even though it was valid a moment ago. The compiler permits that edit because its fields are public. A validation result is evidence about a particular state, not a permanent badge. As more callers appear, remembering every required check becomes harder.
actions: Predict both output lines, then run.
Identify the public operation that invalidates the earlier check.

question.prompt: After title.clear, does the earlier successful valid call still prove the current draft is ready?
question.answer: No. The object has changed. Validation proved the previous state only.

slides.title: Locally valid steps do not prove a valid whole
keyPoints: Both 60-minute additions are accepted
The total is 120 minutes
A final check must precede publication
slides.narration: Each call in this demonstration obeys the rule for one activity and the count limit. Neither call asks whether the complete plan fits ninety minutes. The output therefore shows two accepted steps, a total of one hundred twenty, and false for the final limit. There is no contradiction: we made different promises at different boundaries. A common bug is to assume that successful setters prove the whole product is ready. Our finished design will allow the builder to hold this draft, then refuse to return a Plan from build. A user interface could let the user revise the draft afterward. The builder remains useful even when publication fails.
actions: Predict the three lines before Run.
Ask where a publication function would need its final validation.

question.answer: No. The whole-plan time rule still fails. A publication operation must check the combined state.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Require a nonempty title and 1–3 activities.
Accept activity durations 1–60 minutes and finished totals at most 90.
Keep earlier products unchanged when the builder changes or rejects a step.
slides.narration:
A staged planner that publishes independent snapshots. PlanBuilder stores draft values and alone can call the private Plan constructor after validation. Products own copied data and expose only read access, so partial setup cannot leak through the product API.

Require a nonempty title and 1–3 activities. Accept activity durations 1–60 minutes and finished totals at most 90. Keep earlier products unchanged when the builder changes or rejects a step.

Every successfully built or copied Plan has a title, valid activity count, valid durations, and total at most 90. The builder may be incomplete but never publishes that state as a Plan. Previously built snapshots are independent of later builder changes. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A checked Plan(title, durations) constructor is smaller when all data is available together. A validated factory function also works. The builder is justified by staged input and reusable construction recipes.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Builder implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: Every successfully built or copied Plan has a title, valid activity count, valid durations, and total at most 90. The builder may be incomplete but never publishes that state as a Plan. Previously built snapshots are independent of later builder changes.

slides.title: Why friendship is narrow here
keyPoints: Plan has a private constructor and private data.
The finished Plan exposes a title reference for reading and a computed total.
build returns Plan by value.
slides.narration:
Plan has a private constructor and private data. friend class PlanBuilder grants this one named class access to the private constructor. Friendship is permission, not inheritance, ownership, or automatic trust in every caller. It is not symmetric or transitive. The builder is responsible for checking its draft before using that permission. No other public function in this example can create an invalid Plan by filling fields afterward.

The finished Plan exposes a title reference for reading and a computed total. Its public interface has no setters. Calling title returns a borrowed const string reference, valid only while that Plan remains alive and unchanged by assignment or movement. Returning a copy would provide a simpler lifetime contract at the cost of copying the title. Do not retain the borrowed reference after the plan dies.

build returns Plan by value. The constructor receives a string and vector by value and moves those parameters into its members. Because build itself is const and passes its own members as lvalues, the constructor parameters are copies of the draft. The resulting plan therefore owns independent data. Later builder changes cannot alter earlier products. Plan explicitly defaults its copy constructor. This suppresses implicit move operations, so constructing or assigning it from an rvalue uses copying instead and leaves the source valid. Moving the builder’s temporary constructor parameters into the new product is still safe: those parameters are ordinary local values, not previously published plans. C++17 can construct the returned product directly in its destination; correctness must not depend on counting visible copy calls.

slides.title: Chaining steps does not create magic
keyPoints: named and add return PlanBuilder&, a reference to the same builder.
The member functions check invalid values before changing their vectors or titles.
The program demonstrates two snapshots from one builder.
slides.narration:
named and add return PlanBuilder&, a reference to the same builder. return *this dereferences the implicit this pointer to refer to the current object. This supports builder.named("Practice").add(30).add(30): each call returns the object on which the next call operates. Chaining is an optional convenience. It is not what makes the design Builder; staged construction and the valid-product boundary are the important parts.

The member functions check invalid values before changing their vectors or titles. A rejected add(0) leaves the existing draft unchanged. A fourth activity is rejected even if it would fit the time total, because count and total are separate rules. The maximum sum of a draft is 180, so this example’s int arithmetic cannot overflow on the required compiler platform. A production planner with unbounded counts needs a different bound or checked accumulation.

The program demonstrates two snapshots from one builder. After 30 and 30, first totals 60. Adding another 30 produces second at 90. first still totals 60 because it owns its own copied durations. build does not reset the builder in this design. That policy is part of its contract, not a universal rule. A consuming builder might move data out and require a reset; a reusable builder might return snapshots, as ours does.

slides.title: A director is just a reusable recipe
keyPoints: introduction records a repeated sequence of builder calls.
The broader Builder pattern can use one recipe with different builders to produce different representations, such as an executable session plan and a printed outline.
For a small object with two required values available at once, a checked constructor or a named factory function is simpler.
slides.narration:
introduction records a repeated sequence of builder calls. Such a recipe is called a director in the classic Builder vocabulary. A director does not have to be a class. Here an ordinary function creates a builder, names the plan, adds two activities, and returns the result. The caller receives a Plan without knowing every construction step. If no recipe repeats, callers can drive the builder directly.

The broader Builder pattern can use one recipe with different builders to produce different representations, such as an executable session plan and a printed outline. Those products need not share a base type. A common step interface can express named and add, while each concrete builder exposes its own finished result. A function template can also apply one recipe to builders with matching operations. Introduce that machinery only when the second representation exists; one valid-plan builder does not need an abstract builder hierarchy.

For a small object with two required values available at once, a checked constructor or a named factory function is simpler. A builder becomes valuable when many optional choices accumulate, validation spans choices, or setup order and product readiness need clear separation. A fluent chain of trivial setters on a publicly mutable product does not provide the same guarantee. Ask what invalid state the design prevents, not how attractive the chained syntax looks.

slides.title: build is the gate that turns choices into a promise
keyPoints: named and add collect accepted choices
build checks completeness and total
Only then can the product be constructed
slides.narration: PlanBuilder stores the draft fields privately. named rejects an empty title, and add rejects a bad duration or a fourth activity. build performs the checks that need the assembled draft: a title, at least one activity, and a total at most ninety. It then calls the private Plan constructor. The result is a separate value that the caller may hand to a presenter. This division gives errors a useful location. A zero-minute activity fails at add because no later choice can make that activity valid. A total of one hundred twenty fails at build because it is a property of the assembled plan. The API shows exactly where the stronger promise begins.
actions: Trace a valid draft and an overlong draft to the build boundary.

question.answer: add checks local activity rules. build owns the complete-product contract and must validate the combined draft before returning a Plan.

slides.title: Friendship grants access; it does not perform validation
keyPoints: Plan hides its constructor and data
friend class PlanBuilder grants narrow access
The builder remains responsible for its checks
slides.narration: Private access keeps ordinary callers from filling Plan fields or invoking its checked construction path incorrectly. The friend declaration gives PlanBuilder permission to use the private constructor. That permission is checked during compilation. It does not make the compiler understand the ninety-minute rule, and it does not automatically run validation. A careless new method inside the friend could still call the constructor with bad data. Friendship is therefore a deliberate trust boundary. It is not inheritance: the builder is not a kind of Plan. It is not ownership either. When maintaining this code, review each place that can create a Plan and confirm that it establishes the same invariant.
actions: Point out the private constructor and its friend declaration.
Ask which future changes would widen the trusted construction boundary.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → Why friendship is narrow here

question.prompt: Does friend class PlanBuilder make a builder a subtype of Plan?
question.answer: No. It grants access to private members; it does not create an inheritance relationship or validate values.

slides.title: A snapshot owns its data instead of borrowing the draft
keyPoints: build is const and copies the draft fields
The product owns its title and duration vector
Later builder edits leave earlier plans unchanged
slides.narration: The term snapshot means a value representing the draft at one point in time. build is const, and it passes the draft's string and vector into constructor parameters by value. Those parameters become copies. The constructor moves the temporary parameter values into Plan members, but it does not move the builder's own stored fields out. This distinction explains the chapter's sixty-minute and ninety-minute plans: adding a third activity changes the builder and the second product, while the first remains sixty. Returning by value gives the caller its own Plan. Correctness should not depend on counting copies, since C++ can construct the returned object directly in the destination.
actions: Draw three separate owners: builder, first Plan, second Plan.
Trace where copying happens before the constructor’s moves.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → Why friendship is narrow here

question.prompt: If the constructor uses std::move, why does the original builder still have its choices?
question.answer: The moved values are constructor parameters that were copied from the const builder’s fields. Moving those local copies does not consume the builder.

slides.title: Chaining returns the same builder, not a fresh draft
keyPoints: PlanBuilder& is a reference result
this points to the current object
return *this enables the next call on that same object
slides.narration: In named and add, the result type is PlanBuilder followed by an ampersand. That is a reference to a builder, not a copied builder value. The implicit this pointer identifies the current object; writing *this refers to that object itself. Returning it lets named(...).add(...).add(...) act on one draft in sequence. This fluent syntax is convenient, but it is not the essential Builder idea. The ready-product boundary matters more. Each operation checks a rejected argument before mutating the draft, so add(0) leaves the old state usable. A version returning a copy by mistake could make later chained edits land on temporary drafts and produce surprising results.
actions: Rewrite one chain as three separate statements.
Ask learners to explain why the two forms have the same effect here.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → Chaining steps does not create magic

question.prompt: What does the ampersand in PlanBuilder& change about chained operations?
question.answer: It returns a reference to the current builder, so the next call changes the same draft rather than an unrelated copy.

slides.title: A director is a recipe; reset is a separate policy
keyPoints: introduction repeats a useful sequence
A director can be an ordinary function
The chapter builder retains choices after build
slides.narration: The introduction function names a plan and adds twenty and thirty minutes. It packages a repeated recipe so callers do not need to repeat those steps. In Builder vocabulary, that recipe is a director. A separate director class would add little here, so the chapter uses a function. Another independent choice is what happens after build. Our builder keeps its draft, allowing another snapshot after additional edits. The extension adds reset, which clears only the builder's draft. Existing products keep their own copied data. A builder that consumes its draft can also be reasonable, but clients need a different contract. Never assume that all builders reset or consume just because they share a pattern name.
actions: Describe the director without introducing a new class.
Predict first.total after builder.reset in the extension.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → A director is just a reusable recipe

question.prompt: Should resetting the builder erase the earlier sixty-minute Plan?
question.answer: No. Under this snapshot design, the Plan owns separate data. Reset changes the draft only.

slides.title: Map the roles to the actual types
keyPoints: Builder interface → PlanBuilder::named/add/build
Concrete builder → PlanBuilder
Product → Plan
Director → introduction()
Client → main
slides.narration:
Builder interface → PlanBuilder::named/add/build. Provides construction steps. Our single implementation needs no separate abstract base.

Concrete builder → PlanBuilder. Stores the developing state and performs the actual assembly work.

Product → Plan. Represents the result handed to the caller after construction.

Director → introduction(). Reuses a chosen sequence of steps. A function can perform this role without a director class.

Client → main. Chooses the builder or recipe and receives finished products.

Builder separates staged draft data from valid product objects. Check local rules before each mutation and whole-product rules at build. Define whether build copies, consumes, or resets draft data. A director is a reusable construction recipe and may be a function. Prefer a checked constructor when staged setup solves no real problem.

Place readiness rules at the build boundary and keep the draft type out of execution APIs. Later changes to plan validity then have one obvious place for checks and regression tests.

question.prompt: Explain Builder without reciting its class names.
question.answer: PlanBuilder stores draft values and alone can call the private Plan constructor after validation. Products own copied data and expose only read access, so partial setup cannot leak through the product API. A checked Plan(title, durations) constructor is smaller when all data is available together. A validated factory function also works. The builder is justified by staged input and reusable construction recipes.

slides.title: Separate a useful boundary from attractive syntax
keyPoints: A checked constructor suits a few values known together
Builder suits staged choices and readiness rules
Fluent setters alone do not protect a product
slides.narration: Suppose a type has only a title and one duration, both available at the same call site. A checked constructor may express that requirement clearly with less machinery. Now suppose settings arrive from several screens, have optional values, and must be checked together before use. A builder offers a useful home for the incomplete draft. What does not help is a chain of setters on a publicly mutable finished object if callers can still observe it half-built. The question is not whether calls read like a sentence. Ask which invalid states can cross which boundary, and who is responsible for stopping them. That question connects the pattern to maintainable APIs.

question.prompt: What makes a chain of public product setters weaker than this Builder design?
question.answer: It may leave the same public product observable in incomplete or invalid states; it does not establish a separate checked publication boundary.

slides.title: Test failure without destroying useful state
keyPoints: Rejected step: old draft stays usable
Rejected build: no invalid Plan escapes
Reset: old products remain independent
slides.narration: The best tests inspect what is left after an error, not only whether an error happened. Starting with a valid ninety-minute draft, add(0) should throw and leave the draft able to build the same ninety-minute Plan. A fourth activity should fail for the count rule even if it is only one minute. An overlong draft should fail at build without publishing an invalid product. After reset, build should report an incomplete draft, yet the previously returned Plans should still read correctly. These checks expose accidental mutation before validation, hidden sharing, and an unclear reset policy. They are maintenance tests because future fields and editing operations must preserve the same boundaries.

question.prompt: Why check builder.build().total after add(0) throws?
question.answer: The exception alone does not prove the old draft was preserved. Checking the total verifies that the rejected operation did not corrupt useful state.

slides.title: Explain the draft-to-product boundary in plain words
keyPoints: Collect partial choices in one place
Check local rules on input and whole rules on publication
Publish an independent value
slides.narration: Summarize this chapter as a promise about states. The builder can be unfinished because its job is to collect choices. The Plan must be ready because its job is to be used. build is the checked crossing between them, and the resulting value owns independent data. Now transfer the idea to a report configuration with optional columns and a required destination. Which choices can be rejected immediately? Which need the whole draft? Would the finished report configuration share mutable lists with the builder? These questions help reconstruct the design without memorizing a diagram. The final test is whether another programmer can see the readiness rule from the API and extend it without opening a path around validation.

question.prompt: If a new required field is added, where must its completeness rule be enforced?
